discussionThreads.reason: New competitor claim with essential caveat preserved; current replies verified in logged-out Newest view. Recipe still unresolved.
discussionThreads.summary: mikelou1 reports an 87% local Qwen run under time constraints at roughly four-L4 speed (October 20 03:00 UTC). At 06:26 UTC the same author explicitly says 87% likely will not transfer, would be surprised by even 80%, and hopes for roughly 75%; those are expectations, not a submitted result. A later reply at 08:54 UTC says they are not very concerned about overfit because they get few runs. Other participants discuss throughput and the local-to-leaderboard gap. No complete recipe or independently verified new leaderboard score was supplied.

dispatches.editorNote: Model report checked October 22, 2026. Reflection released Beam on October 16. ARC Prize scores are semi-private evaluations, not Kaggle team standings.
dispatches.headline: Beam’s coding launch meets a tougher grid test: 23.5% on ARC-AGI-2

image.alt: Beam ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2 semi-private scores rise across low, medium, high and xhigh reasoning, with task costs shown for ARC-AGI-2.
image.caption: ARC Daily Digest chart from ARC Prize semi-private data checked October 22, 2026. ARC-AGI-2 task costs range from about ten to sixty-one cents. No ARC-AGI-3 result is listed.

sections.heading: What the verified result says
sections.text: Reflection’s first open-weight model, Beam 1.0, scores 23.5% on ARC-AGI-2 at xhigh reasoning and 74.0% on ARC-AGI-1 at the same setting. ARC Prize’s recorded costs are about 61 cents per ARC-AGI-2 task and 31 cents per ARC-AGI-1 task. The two scores describe substantially different levels of success on two different benchmarks; the older set’s result should not stand in for the newer one. Reflection released the weights on October 16, and this report checks the verified rows on October 22. The page’s release date does not establish the precise publication time of the new evaluations. Beam’s ARC-AGI-2 result leaves considerable room for improvement, even as its launch focuses on coding and sustained agent work.

sections.heading: The useful setting may be below the headline setting
sections.text: ARC-AGI-2 rises from 2.8% at low reasoning to 6.4% at medium, 20.0% at high and 23.5% at xhigh. The corresponding task costs are about $0.10, $0.18, $0.35 and $0.61. Most of the improvement in that ladder arrives before the last setting: high retains a 20% score at roughly 43% lower recorded cost than xhigh. Moving to xhigh buys about three and a half additional percentage points. That is a concrete budget choice, not evidence that either setting is always preferable. The accompanying ARC-AGI-1 ladder is 45.0%, 55.7%, 67.7% and 74.0%. Anyone reproducing Beam should specify the effort setting rather than quote “Beam’s score” as though it were a fixed property independent of inference configuration.

sections.heading: Why the software claims and the ARC result can coexist
sections.text: Reflection’s model card reports 80.1% on Terminal Bench 2.1, 81.6% on SWE-bench Verified and 43.3% on DeepSWE v1.1 for the BF16 release. These are the developer’s reported evaluations. They do not convert into an ARC score. ARC Prize’s policy evaluates ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2 as direct task-to-answer-grid prediction, without an agent harness or client-side tools. Software agents can inspect files, run programs and use execution feedback; these ARC runs ask a different question. Reflection also reports roughly 1.3 billion sandboxes across major reinforcement-learning runs, evaluation and ablations. That is a company-described training operation, not an independently audited count in this report. The evidence supports separate judgments about software workflows and grid-rule generalization; one benchmark’s strength does not erase the other’s limitation.

sections.heading: The release is an engineering stack, not only a checkpoint
sections.text: Beam uses a sparse mixture of experts, with about 501 billion total parameters and 23 billion active per token, a one-million-token context window, and text input and output. Reflection releases BF16, FP8 and NVFP4 weights under Apache 2.0 and also offers a speculative-decoding drafter. Its Mirror CLI provides an inspectable agent environment, and the launch describes integrations for serving, fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. Reflection says Beam was trained with Mirror while also supporting other harnesses. That is relevant to teams interested in modifying the agent as well as the weights. It does not establish that the best coding harness transfers unchanged to ARC. Nor does “23 billion active” mean the entire model has the storage footprint of a dense 23-billion-parameter checkpoint: routing fewer experts for a token and storing the full expert pool are different requirements.

sections.heading: Where Beam belongs in the current ARC picture
sections.text: In the same ARC Prize ARC-AGI-2 snapshot, Muse Spark Open reaches 57.5% at xhigh and DeepSeek Flash 1017 reaches 78.1% at maximum. Their recorded costs are about $0.73 and $0.16 per task respectively, versus Beam’s $0.61. These are comparisons of the published configurations and retail-priced runs, not a controlled study of why the architectures differ. Beam therefore has no accuracy or cost lead over these two alternatives on this particular evaluation. Its inspectable weights and tooling can still make it a research candidate, especially for an experiment that changes the task interface or training recipe. That prospect needs a measured follow-up rather than a promised gain. No ARC-AGI-3 result is listed for Beam. Its text-only interface also makes any future treatment of game frames an explicit harness decision; a missing interactive score means unmeasured, not zero.

dispatches.editorNote: Model report checked October 22, 2026. Release dates and result-check dates are distinct. Scores below are ARC Prize semi-private evaluations, separate from the Kaggle competition.
dispatches.headline: DeepSeek Flash 1017 reaches 78.1% on ARC-AGI-2, with a coverage warning behind the effort curve

image.alt: ARC Prize semi-private scores for DeepSeek Flash 1017 at none, low, high and maximum effort, with the high variant flagged for incomplete coverage.
image.caption: ARC Daily Digest chart from ARC Prize data checked October 22, 2026. High has partial coverage; its cost excludes unrecorded attempts. Costs are per task at recorded retail rates. No ARC-AGI-3 result is listed.

sections.heading: The verified gain
sections.text: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 raises the September checkpoint’s best ARC-AGI-2 score from 72.9% to 78.1% at maximum reasoning: roughly five percentage points of improvement. ARC Prize records about 16 cents per task for the new maximum setting, against about 13 cents for the earlier one. The new checkpoint’s best ARC-AGI-1 figure is 94.5% at high effort; maximum effort scores 93.5% there. Those are different configurations, so the two headline bests should not be presented as one run. DeepSeek released 1017 on October 17. This report checks the verified results on October 22; the release date displayed on the results page does not establish when the evaluation rows first appeared. Among the three models in this series, DeepSeek has the strongest ARC-AGI-2 result.

sections.heading: Read the coverage note before reading the curve
sections.text: The ARC-AGI-2 ladder is 2.1% with reasoning disabled, 73.6% at low, 68.6% at high and 78.1% at maximum. The dip at high is easy to turn into an overthinking story, but ARC Prize’s model metadata explicitly marks that variant as having partial dataset coverage. It says scores use the full catalog denominators while costs include recorded usage only and exclude unrecorded attempts. A published aggregate with missing coverage cannot isolate the effect of extra thinking. Nor does the note identify the missing attempts’ counterfactual answers. The chart therefore marks high with a warning rather than drawing a smooth performance law through it. For practical comparison, retain the coverage qualification alongside the checkpoint, effort and dataset; a score without those conditions conceals the most consequential limitation in this release’s ARC evidence.

sections.heading: Better ARC accuracy is not automatically a cheaper ARC run
sections.text: DeepSeek describes 1017 as completing tasks faster and with shorter outputs, and calls the broader update a performance-and-cost improvement. Its release announcement emphasizes project creation and reinforcement learning with self-feedback. That claim needs to stay attached to the workloads on which the company makes it. In ARC Prize’s recorded maximum-effort ARC-AGI-2 runs, cost rises from roughly $0.129 to $0.163 per task, about a quarter more, while accuracy improves. The low setting costs about $0.134 and scores 73.6%, offering a different point on the tradeoff. ARC Prize uses retail pricing, not the lab’s internal GPU cost, and its policy uses a single run rather than averaging repeats. These observations support a useful accuracy gain; they do not establish cheaper inference for every workload or a universal efficiency win.

sections.heading: What DeepSeek says changed outside ARC
sections.text: The model card reports DeepSWE v1.1 improving from 74.2 to 77.0, Terminal-Bench 4.0 from 31.2 to 42.3, and ProgramBench from 20.3 to 29.1. These are DeepSeek-published comparisons, not additional ARC Prize verification. The card names Mini-SWE-V2 for DeepSWE and Claude Code for Terminal-Bench 4.0. The launch’s project demonstrations include a Godot Portal recreation and 3D scenes; they illustrate the intended end-to-end development use, but are selected demonstrations. The broader research story is an update aimed at carrying a project through execution and feedback, with shorter output as part of the objective. Neither a software benchmark nor a polished demonstration substitutes for testing an unfamiliar grid rule. Conversely, the ARC score alone does not measure the model’s ability to build, debug and ship a repository.

sections.heading: Open weights, protocol fidelity, and the unanswered ARC3 question
sections.text: The checkpoint is available under MIT terms with a one-million-token context recommendation. DeepSeek’s card says there is no Jinja-format chat template and points instead to its reference encoder. Its maintained deepseek-recipe toolkit converts common request formats into DeepSeek conversations and parses thinking, tool calls and images. That matters for reproduction: a wrapper that drops reasoning or misplaces tool content changes the system under test. A serious follow-up should hold the task set and harness fixed, verify the actual checkpoint, and record coverage, failures, token use and cost before attributing differences to the model. This is a proposed experiment, not a run performed for this report. ARC Prize lists no ARC-AGI-3 score for 1017. The September model’s separate interactive results cannot be carried over to this checkpoint. A grid-prediction gain is promising evidence for that task, while interactive exploration remains an open question.

dispatches.editorNote: Model report checked October 22, 2026. Meta released Muse Spark Open on October 15. This is the open checkpoint, not an inherited result for a closed Muse model.
dispatches.headline: Muse Spark Open reaches 57.5% on ARC-AGI-2: capable open weights, a costly top setting

image.alt: Muse Spark Open scores across four reasoning settings: its best ARC-AGI-2 score is 57.5% at xhigh while ARC-AGI-1 reaches 89.0%.
image.caption: ARC Daily Digest chart from ARC Prize semi-private data checked October 22, 2026. The final effort increase adds ten points on ARC-AGI-2 and half a point on ARC-AGI-1. No ARC-AGI-3 result is listed.

sections.heading: A verified result for the open checkpoint
sections.text: Muse Spark Open reaches 57.5% on ARC-AGI-2 and 89.0% on ARC-AGI-1 at xhigh reasoning in ARC Prize’s semi-private evaluations. The recorded per-task costs are about 73 cents and 29 cents respectively. That places it clearly above Beam 1.0 on this grid test, while below DeepSeek Flash 1017’s best ARC-AGI-2 result. Meta released this open checkpoint on October 15; the results here were checked on October 22. The release date shown beside the model is not a timestamp proving when the verified rows first went live. The distinction between this checkpoint and closed Muse versions matters throughout the report: shared branding does not establish identical weights, post-training or benchmark behavior.

sections.heading: What the extra thinking buys
sections.text: Muse Spark Open’s ARC-AGI-2 scores are 12.2% at low, 27.5% at medium, 47.5% at high and 57.5% at xhigh. Its ARC-AGI-1 scores at those settings are 58.5%, 77.7%, 88.5% and 89.0%. The final increase in effort therefore adds only half a point on the older benchmark but ten points on ARC-AGI-2. The harder set is still sensitive to the extra inference configuration even when the older score has nearly flattened. ARC-AGI-2 cost rises from about $0.11 to $0.25, $0.62 and $0.73 across that ladder. At the top, roughly seventeen percent more recorded spending than high accompanies ten additional percentage points. Those are observations from the published runs, not a guarantee that another task mix will deliver the same marginal return.

sections.heading: What Meta actually opened
sections.text: Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a native multimodal mixture-of-experts model with 816 billion total parameters, 42 billion active, and a context window of 1,048,576 tokens. Its documentation lists text, images, audio and video as inputs, with text output. The weights make self-hosting and adaptation possible, but the total expert pool still sets a very large memory requirement. Meta’s launch highlights running the model across two M5 Ultra Mac Studios, alongside conventional hosted and GPU deployment paths. That is a vendor-described configuration, not hardware measured for this report. The release uses the custom Muse Model License with limited commercial terms; it should not be casually described as an Apache- or MIT-licensed release. Meta also says the open version received additional safety post-training for standalone use. Openness here is a concrete deployment choice with its own conditions, rather than a claim that every Muse variant is interchangeable.

sections.heading: Read the wider benchmark table with its methodology
sections.text: Meta’s product table lists 76.4 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the Terminus 2 agent, 60 on DeepSWE 1.1, and 89.2 on MCP-Atlas at xhigh reasoning. Its methodology report explains that the comparison mixes official benchmark-provider results, internal evaluations and some competitors’ self-reported figures. For DeepSWE, it uses each model’s preferred or reported harness; Muse Spark Open’s entry uses Muse Code. For Terminal-Bench, Beam’s figure is self-reported with the harness unspecified in Meta’s account. These distinctions prevent the table from being read as one fully controlled experiment. They also explain why an agentic coding number should retain its harness label. Meta’s agent and perception claims may be useful context for the release, but they remain separate evidence from ARC Prize’s direct grid-prediction test.

sections.heading: What the result changes, and what remains open
sections.text: The ARC result establishes a meaningful rule-generalization capability for a downloadable Meta checkpoint. It does not establish a new lead among the models examined here: DeepSeek Flash 1017 scores higher on ARC-AGI-2 at a substantially lower recorded task cost. Nor does parameter count by itself explain that ordering. Different training, inference settings and serving prices remain part of the comparison. For researchers, Muse Spark Open’s distinctive question is whether access to the multimodal weights and controllable serving stack can produce a better task-specific system. That requires testing the exact checkpoint and harness, and recording what adaptation changes. ARC Prize currently lists no ARC-AGI-3 result for Muse Spark Open; native perception is not an interactive-game score. Its ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2 results should stand on their own while that question remains unmeasured.
